findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are saved as raw (unhashed) codes
findings.body: In createRecoveryCodesCredential, the generatedCodes list is serialized directly into a UserCredentialModel and passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential). Unlike the local-storage path, where recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel) hashes each code (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes the raw codes), the user-storage path stores the raw codes verbatim in the federated credential's challengeResponse/credentialData. Any user-storage provider that persists this value (LDAP attribute, external database, etc.) will hold plaintext recovery codes, which are equivalent to passwords for account recovery. The consequence is that a compromise of the user-storage backend (or its backups/logs) directly yields usable recovery codes, defeating the purpose of hashing them in the local Keycloak DB. The fix is to hash the codes (e.g., via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) before building the UserCredentialModel, matching what the local credential provider does.

findings.title: Test user-storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing raw input against stored values without hashing
findings.body: In isValid(), the recovery-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). Because CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential now sends the raw (unhashed) codes to user storage (see the related finding), this comparison only works because both sides are raw. If the production code is fixed to hash codes before storing them in user storage, this test provider will break; conversely, as written, this provider demonstrates and endorses storing plaintext recovery codes in federated storage. The validation should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode / verifyRecoveryCodeInput) and compare against the stored hashed values, consistent with the local Keycloak credential provider.

findings.title: Recovery codes credential stored in user storage loses userLabel and used-code state
findings.body: In updateCredential(), the recovery-codes branch builds a CredentialModel with only id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON list), and createdDate. It never sets userLabel, and it stores the list of codes as-is, so there is no per-code 'used' flag persisted. getCredentials() later reconstructs the model via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(codes, createdDate, userLabel), which marks all codes as unused. This means a code that was already consumed during login remains valid in user storage: the federated isValid() will keep accepting a used recovery code, allowing unlimited reuse of a single recovery code. The provider must persist and honor the used/unused state (e.g., store the full RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel JSON including per-code used flags, and update it when a code is consumed), otherwise the one-time-use guarantee of recovery codes is broken for federated users.

findings.title: disableCredentialType does not support removing recovery codes from user storage
findings.body: disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (setting myUser.otp = null) and logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type' for everything else, including RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE. Since supportsCredentialType() now advertises recovery-codes support and isConfiguredFor() reports it, the account console/admin REST will list recovery codes as a disableable credential for federated users, but attempting to disable/remove it will silently do nothing (the credential remains in storage and the user can still log in with it). The method should handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE by setting myUser.recoveryCodes = null, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() should include the recovery-codes type when present.

findings.title: Used recovery code is removed by credential ID even when the credential lives in federated user storage
findings.body: After a successful recovery-code login, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used. RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() now returns the federated credential first, and for a federated credential the ID is the one assigned by the user-storage provider (or a dummy id). removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB; for a federated credential this either throws, silently no-ops, or removes nothing, so the consumed-codes state in user storage is never updated. The consequence is that once all codes are used, the federated credential is never invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action logic (which keys off allCodesUsed() on the federated model) may repeatedly trigger or, worse, the storage-side credential keeps accepting codes. The removal path must go through the credential manager's federated-aware removal (e.g., updateCredential with the consumed state, or removeStoredCredentialById only for local credentials), not blindly call removeStoredCredentialById with a federated ID.

findings.title: Optional.get() without isPresent() check will throw NoSuchElementException when no recovery credential exists
findings.body: The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately invokes credentialModelOpt.get() without checking isPresent(). Previously the code used getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get() which had the same latent issue, but now that getCredential() explicitly returns an Optional that can legitimately be empty (federated lookup first, then local), any code path that renders the recovery-code input page for a user without a recovery credential (e.g., a race where the credential was removed, a misconfigured flow, or a user whose credential exists only in a storage provider that doesn't implement getCredentials) will throw NoSuchElementException and produce a 500 error instead of a graceful challenge. The bean should handle the empty case (e.g., throw a meaningful error, disable the input, or fall back), and ideally the template should not render the code-number prompt when no credential exists.

findings.title: getCredential prefers federated credential but ignores local credential when both exist
findings.body: getCredential() returns the first federated recovery-codes credential if present, and only falls back to the local stored credential when no federated one exists. If a user has recovery codes in both the local Keycloak DB (e.g., created before the user was federated, or created by a code path that bypassed the storage check) and in user storage, the local credential is silently ignored: login validation via credentialManager().isValid() may still check both, but the post-login bookkeeping in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (allCodesUsed check and removal) and the code-number display in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean operate only on the federated one. This can lead to inconsistent state where a stale local credential remains valid forever and is never cleaned up, or where the displayed 'next code number' does not match the credential actually being validated. The method should either return all matching credentials or document/enforce a single source of truth, and callers should handle the both-exist case (e.g., prefer local, or remove the stale one).

findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only logs in once with recovery code index 0 and asserts success. It never attempts to reuse the same code (which must fail), never consumes all 12 codes to verify the credential is invalidated/removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered, and never verifies that the used-code state is persisted in the user storage. Given that the production change is specifically about creating and validating recovery codes in user storage, the absence of these assertions leaves the core security property (codes are single-use and the credential lifecycle works for federated users) untested. The test should reuse a consumed code and assert failure, and ideally drive the flow until all codes are used.
